This confirms the F->Fullscreen binding is wired end-to-end.
fullscreen.headlessLimitation: Headless Chromium refuses to actually enter OS-level fullscreen (no display, no user gesture), so we assert on the API invocation rather than on document.fullscreenElement. In a real browser session F correctly transitions the deck root into browser fullscreen.

knownLimitations: Fullscreen entry via 'F' cannot be observed in headless Chromium as an actual OS-level fullscreen transition; verification asserts on requestFullscreen being invoked on '.reveal-full-page', which is the documented reveal.js v6 behavior (shown in its built-in help overlay).

The deck uses reveal.js's native 16:9 scaling (width:1600, height:900, margin:0.04). It intentionally does NOT wrap that in a custom fixed-stage scaler — reveal.js already does the scaling, and layering another one would fight it.

The supplemental deck.css relies on setting Reveal.initialize({ display: 'flex' }) so that reveal.js inlines display:flex on the current slide (matching the flex layouts declared in deck.css). Changing display back to 'block' would break vertical centering on the title (slide 1), demo (slide 9), and closing (slide 11) slides.
Only English 'primary' narration lines from script.json are placed into <aside class="notes"> — the Chinese 'secondary' lines are omitted from speaker notes, matching typical Speaker View usage.
No fragments, no vertical slide stacks, no markdown source — every slide is a single top-level <section> to keep the deck.js/notes/overview verifications simple and unambiguous.
